proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(q=(1-\alpha)/2\).  Uniform coverage of \(I_{T,\Delta}\) over \(\mathfrak M_T(\alpha,\beta,L,c,C,\varepsilon)\) follows directly from \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}gated\text{-}inference}\), because that theorem is unconditional on quota success and is uniform over the union containing this class.  We prove the expected-length assertion and the two converse components.

\emph{Upper bound.}
By \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\), uniformly over the class,
\[
 K_1(n_T)\asymp T^{1-\alpha},\qquad
 K_0(n_T)\asymp T,
 \qquad J_1\asymp T^{\rho(1-\alpha)},\qquad
 J_0\asymp T^\rho. \tag{1}
\]
Thus, for the quantities in \(\mathrm{def:hybrid\text{-}interval}\),
\[
 S_T=K_1(n_T)^{-1}+K_0(n_T)^{-1}
     =O\!\left(T^{-(1-\alpha)}\right),
 \qquad
 a_T=\sqrt{2S_Tx_\eta}=O(T^{-q}). \tag{2}
\]
The cohort schedule gives \(g_{T,\Delta}=m_T+\Delta_T\geq m_T\asymp T^\rho\).  Hence the polynomial delay envelope in the model-class definition yields
\[
 v_{T,\Delta}
 =\min\{1,L(1+g_{T,\Delta})^{-\beta}\}
 =O(T^{-\rho\beta}). \tag{3}
\]
For every fixed \(x>0\), equations (1)--(3) and the definition
\(
A_{a,T,\Delta}(x)=\sqrt{2v_{T,\Delta}x/J_a}+4x/(3J_a)
\)
give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A_{1,T,\Delta}(x)
 &=O\!\left(T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)/2}
          +T^{-\rho(1-\alpha)}\right),\\
 A_{0,T,\Delta}(x)
 &=O\!\left(T^{-\rho(\beta+1)/2}+T^{-\rho}\right).
 \end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
The declared restriction
\(
\rho>(1-\alpha)/(1-\alpha+\beta)
\)
implies \(\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)>1-\alpha\), while \(\rho>1/2\) implies \(\rho(1-\alpha)>(1-\alpha)/2=q\).  Also
\(
(1-\alpha)/(1-\alpha+\beta)\geq(1-\alpha)/(1+\beta)
\), so \(\rho(1+\beta)>1-\alpha\), and \(\rho>1/2\geq q\).  Consequently both lines of (4) are \(o(T^{-q})\).  These inequalities are strict, so the same calculation absorbs the factor \(\log T\) when \(x=4\log T\), proving
\[
 d_{T,\Delta}
 =A_{1,T,\Delta}(4\log T)+A_{0,T,\Delta}(4\log T)
 =o(T^{-q}). \tag{5}
\]

Every main-prefix variable lies in \([-1,1]\).  Since each quota is at least two, its usual unbiased sample variance is at most two.  Therefore, on \(E_T\),
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2\leq2S_T,
 \qquad \widehat s_{T,\Delta}=O(T^{-q}). \tag{6}
\]
Let \(z=\Phi^{-1}(1-\eta/2)\).  For \(u\geq0\), evaluating the defining coverage function of \(c_\eta(u)\) at \(u+z\) gives
\[
 \Phi(z)+\Phi(2u+z)-1\geq2\Phi(z)-1=1-\eta.
\]
That coverage function is increasing in its critical-value argument, so uniqueness in \(\mathrm{def:bounded\text{-}shift\text{-}critical\text{-}value}\) implies
\[
 c_\eta(u)\leq u+z,
 \qquad
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}c_\eta(B_{T,\Delta}/\widehat s_{T,\Delta})
 \leq B_{T,\Delta}+z\widehat s_{T,\Delta} \tag{7}
\]
whenever \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}>0\); the zero-standard-error case uses the concentration branch by definition.

Next, \(h_{T,\Delta}=H_T-k_T\), \(H_T\geq T\), and \(k_T=O(T^\rho)\) with \(\rho<1\).  Therefore
\[
 \frac{1+h_{T,\Delta}}{1+H_T}
 =1-\frac{k_T}{1+H_T}=1+o(1) \tag{8}
\]
uniformly over all deterministic \(\Delta_T\geq0\).  The bias-radius definition then gives
\[
 B_{T,\Delta}=O\!\left((1+H_T)^{-\beta}\right). \tag{9}
\]
Equations (2), (4), and (9) bound the concentration-branch radius by a constant multiple of
\(
r_{T,\Delta}=\max\{T^{-q},(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}
\).
Equations (5)--(7) and (9) give the same bound for the Gaussian-branch radius.  Intersection with \([-2,2]\) cannot increase length.  On \(E_T^c\), the interval has length four, and \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\) gives
\[
 4P(E_T^c)\leq16T^{-4}=o(T^{-q})=o(r_{T,\Delta}). \tag{10}
\]
Taking expectations proves the stated uniform upper bound.

\emph{Sampling converse.}
Fix the same deterministic policy in both experiments:
\[
 p_t:=\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha},
 \qquad \pi_t(0)=1-p_t. \tag{11}
\]
It is admissible for \(\mathfrak M_T(\alpha,\beta,L,c,C,\varepsilon)\): the rare-arm lower bound holds with equality, the upper bound follows from \(c\leq C\), and deterministic randomization with probability \(p_t\) satisfies sequential randomization.  Notice that no upper allocation bound is used after this membership check.  Set both delays to zero and set \(Y_t(0)=0\).  Under \(P_+\) and \(P_-\), respectively, let the independent and identically distributed arm-one outcome be Rademacher with means \(d_T\) and \(-d_T\), where
\[
 Q_T=\sum_{t=1}^T p_t,
 \qquad d_T=\lambda Q_T^{-1/2},
 \qquad 0<\lambda<\frac{1-2\eta}{4\sqrt2}. \tag{12}
\]
Because \(\alpha<1\), integral comparison gives \(Q_T\asymp T^{1-\alpha}\), and hence \(d_T\asymp T^{-q}\) and \(d_T<1\) for all sufficiently large \(T\).  The outcomes are bounded, the delays satisfy the polynomial envelope, and the two causal contrasts are
\(
\tau_+=d_T
\)
and
\(
\tau_-=-d_T
\).

The assignment and logged-propensity laws are common to the two experiments.  Given an arm-zero assignment, the observed-record laws agree; given an arm-one assignment, the Hellinger affinity of the two Rademacher laws is \(\sqrt{1-d_T^2}\).  Independence of the arrival vectors and the deterministic policy in (11) thus give the exact affinity of the observed experiments:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Aff}(P_+^O,P_-^O)
 &=\prod_{t=1}^T
   \left[1-p_t\{1-\sqrt{1-d_T^2}\}\right]\\
 &\geq1-\sum_{t=1}^T p_td_T^2
 =1-\lambda^2. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{13}
\]
Here \(1-\sqrt{1-x}\leq x\) for \(x\in[0,1]\), and
\(
\prod_t(1-x_t)\geq1-\sum_t x_t
\)
for \(x_t\in[0,1]\).  For any two dominated laws with densities \(p\) and \(q\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 &=\frac12\int|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\\
 &\leq\frac12
 \left\{\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2
       \int(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2\right\}^{1/2}
 =\sqrt{1-\operatorname{Aff}(P,Q)^2}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{14}
\]
Equations (13)--(14) imply
\[
 \|P_+^O-P_-^O\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq\sqrt{1-(1-\lambda^2)^2}
 \leq\sqrt2\lambda. \tag{15}
\]

Let \(J_{T,\Delta}\) have the asserted uniform coverage; equivalently, allow a sequence \(\gamma_T\to0\) such that each of these two laws has coverage at least \(1-\eta-\gamma_T\).  Transferring the coverage of \(\tau_-\) from \(P_-^O\) to \(P_+^O\), then applying the union bound and (15), yields
\[
 P_+^O\{\tau_+,\tau_-\in J_{T,\Delta}\}
 \geq1-2\eta-2\gamma_T-\sqrt2\lambda. \tag{16}
\]
The right-hand side is eventually bounded below by a positive constant depending only on \(\eta\).  On this event the interval has length at least \(2d_T\).  Thus (12) and \(Q_T\asymp T^{1-\alpha}\) imply
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|J_{T,\Delta}|
 \geq c_{\eta,1}T^{-q} \tag{17}
\]
for a constant \(c_{\eta,1}>0\).  This calculation uses a single fixed admissible policy; it neither requires nor exploits the upper allocation envelope beyond placing that policy in the displayed subclass.

\emph{Hidden-tail converse.}
Retain the policy (11) and put
\[
 \delta_T=\min\{1/4,L(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}. \tag{18}
\]
For each recruitment time and arm, draw a Bernoulli indicator of probability \(\delta_T\), independently over recruitment times.  On failure set \((Y_t(a),D_t(a))=(0,0)\); on success set \(D_t(a)=H_T+1\).  Under \(P_+\), give a successful arm-one observation outcome \(+1\) and a successful arm-zero observation outcome \(-1\); under \(P_-\), reverse these signs.  Any dependence between the two arms within an arrival vector may be fixed identically under the two laws.  The arrival vectors are independent and identically distributed over \(t\), and the outcomes are bounded.  For every integer \(u\geq0\),
\[
 P_\pm\{D_t(a)>u\}
 =\begin{cases}
 \delta_T,&0\leq u\leq H_T,\\
 0,&u\geq H_T+1,
 \end{cases}
 \leq\min\{1,L(1+u)^{-\beta}\}. \tag{19}
\]
Thus the laws belong to the model class and all delays are finite.

No successful atom is revealed by terminal time \(H_T\).  The immediate zero records, nonrevelation indicators, assignments, and logged propensities therefore have exactly the same joint law under \(P_+\) and \(P_-\), so the complete observed laws of \(O_{T,\Delta}\) coincide.  Their eventual causal contrasts nevertheless are
\[
 \tau_+=2\delta_T,
 \qquad \tau_-=-2\delta_T. \tag{20}
\]
Under the common observed law, uniform coverage and a union bound give
\[
 P\{\tau_+,\tau_-\in J_{T,\Delta}\}
 \geq1-2\eta-2\gamma_T. \tag{21}
\]
On this event the interval length is at least \(4\delta_T\).  Since \(H_T\geq T\to\infty\), equation (18) equals \(L(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\) eventually.  Hence
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|J_{T,\Delta}|
 \geq c_{\eta,2}(1+H_T)^{-\beta} \tag{22}
\]
for some \(c_{\eta,2}>0\).  The witness deliberately couples the nonzero outcome to the long delay, so this tail converse does not assert a lower bound within an outcome--delay-independence subclass.

The affinity identity (13) and the indistinguishability identity preceding (20) hold at every finite horizon, including \(T\leq4\); thus the same-experiment stress test does not condition on quota success, propensity convergence, or recruitment success.  Combining (17) and (22), and using
\[
 \max\{c_{\eta,1}x,c_{\eta,2}y\}
 \geq\min\{c_{\eta,1},c_{\eta,2}\}\max\{x,y\},
\]
proves the lower bound at
\(
r_{T,\Delta}=\max\{T^{-q},(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\}
\).
When \(\Delta_T=0\), \(H_T=T\), which gives
\(
\max\{T^{-(1-\alpha)/2},T^{-\beta}\}
\), as claimed.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The one-sided forced-exploration class is the paper's primary minimax class after the established stronger frontier theorem, rather than merely a comparison class.

proposed.name: Primary one-sided forced-exploration minimax class
proposed.construction: \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)=\{(P,\Pi,T):\text{ass:iid-arrivals, ass:bounded-outcomes, ass:polynomial-delay-envelope, ass:sequential-randomization, ass:one-sided-forced-exploration, and ass:control-floor hold at index }T\}\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The descriptive name must match the established role of this unchanged mathematical class as the primary minimax domain.

prose_updates.tldr: Under the anchor's one-sided polynomial allocation condition \(\pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha}\), together with an explicit control-arm floor, a measurable two-cohort gate-and-fallback interval has exact class-minimax expected-length order \(\max\{T^{-(1-\alpha)/2},(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\}\) for the eventual arm-mean contrast. The result extends beyond the anchor's outcome--delay-independence model by allowing arbitrary dependence between each bounded outcome and its finite delay subject to the known polynomial tail envelope. A fixed admissible policy supplies both converse experiments; the ordinary-Wald boundary is the vanishing tail-envelope-to-standard-error ratio, and the bounded-shift Gaussian calibration is attained at the phase boundary.

project_justification.gap: Delayed adaptive-inference theory supplies the one-sided forced-exploration design condition but centers scores under outcome--delay independence; reward-dependent-delay work supplies regret lower bounds rather than uniformly honest interval-length theory for an eventual causal contrast.
project_justification.niche: The missing design-based object is the exact expected-length frontier under the one-sided exploration allocation regime with a control floor when logged propensities may oscillate, revelation is informative, and prespecified post-recruitment follow-up changes the observable endpoint set.
project_justification.fill: The project combines an unconditional arm-tape reduction, deterministic two-cohort prefixes, an observable variance gate with a concentration fallback, and same-policy prompt-tilt and hidden-sign experiments to prove the one-sided class-minimax frontier, the ordinary-Wald boundary, the attained bounded-shift calibration, and the follow-up elbow.

sampling_model.treatment: The prespecified rare arm satisfies \(\pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha}\), and the control arm satisfies \(\pi_t(0)\geq\varepsilon\). Policies may allocate the designated rare arm more often than order \(t^{-\alpha}\). The former two-sided comparability class is retained as a convenient contained subclass because \(ct^{-\alpha}\leq\pi_t(1)\leq Ct^{-\alpha}\) and \(C\leq1-\varepsilon\) imply the control floor.
sampling_model.overlap: The primary minimax class uses the one-sided polynomial forced-exploration floor together with the control-arm floor. Lower-envelope quotas give policy-uniform achievability without convergence of \(t^\alpha\pi_t(1)\), while the single fixed policy \(\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha}\) lies in both the primary class and the two-sided subclass and fixes the hard information order for both converse components.

prose_updates.related_work: Shi, Wang, and Wu provide the design-side anchor through a one-sided polynomial forced-exploration condition. The present result uses that allocation condition together with an explicit control floor and extends inference to outcome-dependent delays. It does not claim that its hidden-tail converse is a result for the anchor's outcome--delay-independence model: the prompt-outcome sampling converse is compatible with independence, whereas the hidden-sign witness deliberately is not. Hadad et al. and Bibaut et al. develop predictable weighting and variance stabilization for prompt outcomes. Manegueu et al. and Vernade et al. motivate polynomial delay-tail control under more restrictive delay structures. Lancewicki et al. and Tang, Wang, and Zheng analyze reward-dependent-delay bias and regret rather than interval length. Bai, Hu, and Rosenberger and Ma, Wang, and Wei obtain classical delayed response-adaptive asymptotics under ignorable-delay conditions. Armstrong and Kolesár provide the bounded-bias Gaussian calibration adapted to the attained boundary here. Liberali et al. are the cardiovascular-trial consumer: their real-time delayed-endpoint intervals require either a tail pad or follow-up sufficient for the uniform boundary unless a stronger prompt or ignorable-delay law is separately certified.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The rate-order frontier, uniform gate theorem, and attained bounded-shift calibration are proved, but exact normalized expected-length constants and the globally optimal variable-length or randomized interval remain open. The construction intentionally discards assignments beyond deterministic quotas; it attains the exact class-minimax rate order but is not claimed constant-efficient for policies that explore more aggressively. Uniform validity uses a known tail envelope, independent and identically distributed stationary arrival vectors, bounded outcomes, finite delays implied by the polynomial envelope, a control-arm floor, and a prespecified terminal time. Unknown envelope parameters, cross-arrival dependence, and nonstationary endpoint rates are outside scope.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The exact minimax order is over the one-sided forced-exploration class with a control-arm floor; the two-sided comparable-policy theorem is retained as a convenient subclass result, not because its upper envelope is needed for the sampling converse. The same fixed policy \(\pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha}\) is used in both lower-bound pairs. The sampling converse is compatible with outcome--delay independence, but the informative hidden-sign tail converse is deliberately outside that independence subclass. On regular-variance sequences, ordinary Wald is uniformly honest exactly when \(T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\to0\), where \(q=(1-\alpha)/2\). Consequently no follow-up is needed when \(\beta>q\); when \(\beta=q\), one needs \(\Delta_T/T\to\infty\); and when \(\beta<q\), one needs \(T+\Delta_T\gg T^{q/\beta}\). Outside this boundary the bias-aware Gaussian branch or concentration fallback supplies coverage. Application to a particular cardiovascular trial still requires an audit of stationarity, logged propensities, the tail envelope, terminal ascertainment, and the risk-difference estimand.

statement_notes.justification: This two-sided theorem is retained as a convenient subclass presentation of the rate frontier. Its achievability uses only the lower allocation envelope, and the fixed-policy prompt-tilt and hidden-sign witnesses establish its converse while also transferring the same lower bound to the larger one-sided class; the rare-arm upper envelope is not needed for either testing argument.
statement_notes.gap: The one-sided forced-exploration regime in Shi, Wang, and Wu is paired there with outcome--delay independence, not with an exact uniformly honest interval-length frontier under informative delay. The prompt sampling witness remains compatible with their independence restriction, whereas the hidden-sign tail witness deliberately falls outside it; Lancewicki et al. establish indistinguishability for regret rather than interval length.
statement_notes.consumer: Investigators can treat this retained two-sided result as a convenient subclass guarantee while using the stronger one-sided theorem to translate an exploration floor, control floor, and endpoint-tail audit into the shortest defensible order of uncertainty.

proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\mathrm{thm:one\text{-}sided\text{-}minimax\text{-}length\text{-}frontier}\), applied to the same class \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\), the same prespecified deterministic follow-up sequence \(\Delta_T\), and the interval constructed in \(\mathrm{def:hybrid\text{-}interval}\), there is a finite constant \(C_\eta\), depending only on the fixed class parameters and \(\eta\), such that
\[
 \inf_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)}
 P\{\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}\}\geq 1-\eta-o(1)
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T)\in\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)}
 \mathbb E_{P,\Pi}|I_{T,\Delta}|
 \leq C_\eta r_{T,\Delta}.
\]
The first displayed inequality is precisely uniform asymptotic honesty over the one-sided class: the infimum is taken over the entire class, so its remainder is uniform rather than pointwise.  The second displayed inequality is precisely the claimed uniform expected-length bound.

It remains only to identify the construction in these inequalities with the one asserted in the proposition.  By \(\mathrm{def:one\text{-}sided\text{-}policy\text{-}class}\), the class imposes the arm-one lower allocation condition \(\pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha}\) and the control floor \(\pi_t(0)\geq\varepsilon\), but no upper rare-arm envelope.  The theorem uses the deterministic quotas generated from these two lower envelopes and the interval \(I_{T,\Delta}\) of \(\mathrm{def:hybrid\text{-}interval}\).  Hence its two conclusions apply to exactly the quotas and interval named here, proving the proposition without any two-sided comparability condition.

proposed.statement: Uniformly over \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\), the deterministic lower-envelope quotas and the interval \(I_{T,\Delta}\) are uniformly honest and have expected length at most a constant multiple of \(r_{T,\Delta}\).
proposed.justification: This proposition extracts the constructive upper half of the exact class-minimax theorem on the one-sided policy class. Together with the same-experiment converse in the one-sided minimax-length theorem, it yields the exact frontier without a rare-arm upper allocation envelope.
proposed.gap: Shi, Wang, and Wu study one-sided forced exploration for delayed asymptotic inference under outcome--delay independence. Here the one-sided arm-one allocation floor and explicit control floor are retained while outcome and delay may be dependent, and the policy-uniform construction participates in an exact class-minimax result. The sampling converse is compatible with outcome--delay independence, whereas the hidden-sign tail converse deliberately uses informative delays.
proposed.consumer: Analysts whose logs certify the arm-one forced-exploration floor and the control-arm floor may use the hybrid interval as a uniformly honest, rate-optimal interval over the full one-sided policy class; two-sided propensity comparability is not required for the exact frontier.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The round-3 directive requires the target-local justification, gap, and consumer metadata to reflect the already-proved exact minimax frontier on the one-sided class; the mathematical claim and dependency spine are unchanged.

added_lemmas.statement:
Consider a stationary independent binary-endpoint experiment with predictable sequential randomization, logged propensities satisfying \(\pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha}\) and \(\pi_t(0)\geq\varepsilon\), and potential delays satisfying \(P\{D_t(a)>u\}\leq\min\{1,L(1+u)^{-\beta}\}\).  The armwise risk difference is the causal contrast \(\tau=P Y_t(1)-P Y_t(0)\).  From records observed through \(H_T=T+\Delta_T\), compute \(\widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}\) and its intervals as defined above.  Uniform asymptotic honesty of the unpadded ordinary-Wald interval \(I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm W}\) over the one-sided policy class \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\) requires
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad q=(1-\alpha)/2.
\]
On the regular subclass \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\), this condition is also sufficient for ordinary Wald.  Without the regular-variance condition, the uniformly honest choice is the measurable hybrid \(I_{T,\Delta}\), which uses the bias-aware Gaussian interval only on the observable gate \(G_{T,\Delta}\) and otherwise uses the concentration interval; with the same quota-failure convention, the concentration interval may instead be used alone.  With no extra follow-up, the displayed condition holds when \(\beta>q\).  When \(\beta=q\), it holds if and only if \(\Delta_T/T\to\infty\); when \(\beta<q\), it holds if and only if \(T+\Delta_T\gg T^{q/\beta}\).  Necessity is class-wide rather than pointwise: prompt-delay laws with \(b_{T,\Delta}=0\) may admit ordinary-Wald inference.  The hidden-tail witness used for the tail necessity deliberately permits outcome--delay dependence, whereas the separate sampling-rate converse is compatible with outcome--delay independence.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Because a binary endpoint satisfies \(Y_t(a)\in\{0,1\}\subset[-1,1]\), the support condition holds.  The stationary independent sampling and predictable sequential-randomization conditions in the statement are exactly the corresponding sampling and design assumptions.  Together with
\[
 \pi_t(1)\geq ct^{-\alpha},\qquad \pi_t(0)\geq\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 P\{D_t(a)>u\}\leq\min\{1,L(1+u)^{-\beta}\},
 \tag{1}
\]
the definition of \(\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\) therefore puts the experiment directly in the one-sided policy class.  No upper bound on \(\pi_t(1)\) is used in this inclusion.  Moreover, for a binary endpoint,
\[
 P Y_t(1)-P Y_t(0)
 =P\{Y_t(1)=1\}-P\{Y_t(0)=1\}=\tau,
 \tag{2}
\]
so the reported risk difference is the stated causal contrast, rather than merely an observed-law regression functional.

The estimator and all three interval branches are measurable functions of \(O_{T,\Delta}\).  Indeed, assignments determine tape order and the quota event \(E_T\); for each recruited unit, the recorded revelation time determines whether its response contributes to \(X_{a,j}^{\Delta}\) or \(R_{a,j}^{\Delta}\); and the definitions prescribe zero for an absent response and \([-2,2]\) on quota failure.  Thus this construction neither conditions on quota success nor requires a limit for \(t^\alpha\pi_t(1)\).

For completeness, the concentration-only recommendation follows directly from the fixed-tape representation.  Write \(K_a=K_a(n_T)\), \(J_a=K_a(k_T)\), and let \(\widetilde\tau_{T,\Delta}\) denote the unconditional virtual estimator formed from these fixed tape prefixes, before applying the quota-failure convention.  If \(Z\) is centered and lies in an interval of length \(r\), convexity of the exponential gives
\[
 E e^{\lambda Z}\leq \exp(\lambda^2r^2/8).
 \tag{3}
\]
To verify (3), bound \(e^{\lambda z}\) by the chord joining its endpoint values, take expectations using \(EZ=0\), and differentiate the logarithm of the resulting two-point expression twice; its second derivative is at most \(r^2/4\), while its value and first derivative at zero are zero.  Applied to the independent tape variables with coefficients \(K_1^{-1}\) and \(-K_0^{-1}\), (3) yields
\[
 P\!\left(\left|(M_{1,\Delta}-EM_{1,\Delta})-(M_{0,\Delta}-EM_{0,\Delta})\right|>
 \sqrt{2S_Tx}\right)\leq2e^{-x},
 \quad S_T=K_1^{-1}+K_0^{-1}.
 \tag{4}
\]
For \(R=Y\mathbf 1\{g_{T,\Delta}<D\leq h_{T,\Delta}\}\), boundedness and the delay envelope give
\[
 |R|\leq1,\qquad E R^2\leq P\{D>g_{T,\Delta}\}\leq v_{T,\Delta}.
 \tag{5}
\]
If \(Z=R-ER\), then \(|Z|\leq2\), and expansion of the exponential, the inequalities \(|EZ^j|\leq2^{j-2}EZ^2\) for \(j\geq2\) and \(j!\geq2\,3^{j-2}\), and \(1+y\leq e^y\) show, for \(0\leq\lambda<3/2\),
\[
 E e^{\lambda Z}
 \leq \exp\!\left\{\frac{\lambda^2EZ^2}{2(1-2\lambda/3)}\right\}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Chernoff's inequality applied to (6), first with \(\lambda\) and then with \(-\lambda\), gives for each arm
\[
 P\!\left(\left|U_{a,\Delta}-EU_{a,\Delta}\right|>
 \sqrt{\frac{2v_{T,\Delta}x}{J_a}}+\frac{4x}{3J_a}\right)\leq2e^{-x}.
 \tag{7}
\]
The linear term in (7) is weakly larger than the optimized Bernstein term, so the displayed inequality follows from (6).  By the arm-tape equivalence, the samples used above are independent fixed prefixes even when outcome and delay are dependent.  The old-cohort correction identity gives
\[
 E\widetilde\tau_{T,\Delta}=\tau-b_{T,\Delta},
 \qquad |b_{T,\Delta}|\leq B_{T,\Delta}.
 \tag{8}
\]
On \(E_T\), the observed estimator equals \(\widetilde\tau_{T,\Delta}\).  Combining (4), the two instances of (7), and (8), and taking \(x=x_\eta=\log(6/\eta)\), a union bound therefore gives
\[
 P\{\tau\notin I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{conc}}\text{ on }E_T\}
 \leq 2e^{-x_\eta}+2e^{-x_\eta}+2e^{-x_\eta}=\eta.
 \tag{9}
\]
On \(E_T^c\) the prescribed interval is \([-2,2]\), which contains \(\tau\) by (2).  Hence the concentration fallback is honest without conditioning on \(E_T\).  The uniform gated-inference theorem additionally proves uniform honesty of the hybrid interval and, on \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\), the uniform studentized approximation and consistency of \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}\).

We next verify that the necessity invoked by a binary-endpoint protocol is not an artifact of outcomes taking values in \([-1,1]\).  Let
\[
 x_T=T^q(1+H_T)^{-\beta},\qquad
 \delta_T=\min\left\{\frac14,\frac L2(1+H_T)^{-\beta}\right\},
 \tag{10}
\]
and use the deterministic policy
\[
 \pi_t(1)=ct^{-\alpha},\qquad \pi_t(0)=1-ct^{-\alpha}\geq1-c\geq\varepsilon.
 \tag{11}
\]
For a sign \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), put \((r_1^\sigma,r_0^\sigma)=(1,0)\) when \(\sigma=1\) and \((r_1^\sigma,r_0^\sigma)=(0,1)\) when \(\sigma=-1\).  Independently over arrivals, define the arm-\(a\) law by
\[
 (D(a),Y(a))=
 \begin{cases}
 (H_T+1,r_a^\sigma),&\text{with probability }\delta_T,\\
 (0,Z_a^\sigma),&\text{with probability }1-\delta_T,
 \end{cases}
 \quad
 Z_a^\sigma\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(
 \frac{1/2-\delta_T r_a^\sigma}{1-\delta_T}\right).
 \tag{12}
\]
Since \(0<\delta_T\leq1/4\), both Bernoulli probabilities in (12) belong to \([0,1]\).  For \(0\leq u\leq H_T\),
\[
 P\{D(a)>u\}=\delta_T
 \leq \frac L2(1+H_T)^{-\beta}
 \leq L(1+u)^{-\beta},
 \tag{13}
\]
and for \(u\geq H_T+1\) this probability is zero.  Thus (12) obeys the polynomial delay envelope.  Direct calculation gives
\[
 E Y(a)=\delta_T r_a^\sigma+(1-\delta_T)
 \frac{1/2-\delta_T r_a^\sigma}{1-\delta_T}=\frac12,
 \qquad \operatorname{Var}\{Y(a)\}=\frac14.
 \tag{14}
\]
Consequently \(\tau=0\), whereas the response visible by \(H_T\) has mean \(1/2-\delta_T r_a^\sigma\).  Because the delayed component in (12) has delay \(H_T+1>h_{T,\Delta}\), it enters neither cohort correction, and therefore
\[
 b_{T,\Delta}=\delta_T(r_1^\sigma-r_0^\sigma)=\sigma\delta_T.
 \tag{15}
\]
This is a finite-delay, binary-outcome member of the same one-sided experiment.  It deliberately makes delay informative through (12).

The deterministic quota formula and \(n_T/T\to1\) imply
\[
 K_1(n_T)\sim\frac{c}{1-\alpha}T^{1-\alpha},
 \qquad K_0(n_T)\sim\varepsilon T.
 \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, \(\sum_{t\leq n_T}t^{-\alpha}\sim n_T^{1-\alpha}/(1-\alpha)\), and the square-root subtraction in the quota is \(o(Q_a(n_T))\).  Under (12), \(P\{X_{a,1}^{\Delta}=1\}=1/2-\delta_T r_a^\sigma\to1/2\), so (16) gives, for a constant \(\gamma\in(0,\infty)\),
\[
 T^q s_{T,\Delta}\longrightarrow\gamma,
 \quad
 \gamma^2=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\alpha)/(4c),&\alpha>0,\\
 (c^{-1}+\varepsilon^{-1})/4,&\alpha=0.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{17}
\]
Since \(H_T\geq T\to\infty\), the second term in the minimum in (10) is eventually active.  Hence
\[
 \frac{|b_{T,\Delta}|}{s_{T,\Delta}}
 =\frac{L}{2\gamma}x_T\{1+o(1)\}.
 \tag{18}
\]
The family in (12) belongs to the regular subclass with variance-floor parameter \(\kappa_0=1/4\) when \(\alpha>0\), and with \(\kappa_0=1/2\) when \(\alpha=0\), by (14).  The uniform studentized theorem applied with this fixed feasible \(\kappa_0\), together with (15), yields
\[
 \frac{\widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau}{\widehat s_{T,\Delta}}
 \ \Rightarrow\ N(-\sigma u,1)
 \tag{19}
\]
along every subsequence on which the right-hand side of (18) tends to \(u\in(0,\infty)\); if it diverges, the absolute shift diverges in probability.  For \(z=z_{1-\eta/2}\), the limiting coverage in the finite-shift case is
\[
 \Phi(z-u)+\Phi(z+u)-1<2\Phi(z)-1=1-\eta,
 \tag{20}
\]
where strictness follows because the derivative in \(u>0\) is \(\phi(z+u)-\phi(z-u)<0\).  In the divergent-shift case the coverage tends to zero.  If \(x_T\not\to0\), it has either a subsequence bounded away from zero with a further finite positive limit, or an unbounded subsequence; (19)--(20) then disprove uniform honesty of ordinary Wald.  This establishes the asserted necessary condition on the full one-sided policy class.  The ordinary-Wald follow-up proposition supplies the converse implication on \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\): when \(x_T\to0\), ordinary Wald is uniformly asymptotically honest.

It remains only to solve the deterministic follow-up inequality.  Since \(q=(1-\alpha)/2>0\), when \(\Delta_T=0\) and \(\beta>q\),
\[
 T^q(1+T)^{-\beta}\sim T^{q-\beta}\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{21}
\]
When \(\beta=q\),
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-q}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{1+T+\Delta_T}{T}\longrightarrow\infty
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{\Delta_T}{T}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{22}
\]
When \(\beta<q\), positivity permits taking the \(\beta\)-th root, and \(q/\beta>1\), so
\[
 T^q(1+T+\Delta_T)^{-\beta}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{1+T+\Delta_T}{T^{q/\beta}}\longrightarrow\infty
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T+\Delta_T\gg T^{q/\beta}.
 \tag{23}
\]
Finally, a prompt-delay law has \(D(a)=0\) and hence \(b_{T,\Delta}=0\); the hidden-tail shift in (18) is then absent.  Thus the necessity above is a uniform class statement and does not assert failure at every law.  The sampling component of the one-sided minimax-length theorem uses prompt delays and is therefore compatible with outcome--delay independence; only the hidden-tail construction (12), which proves the tail obstruction relevant here, uses outcome--delay dependence.
